now.label: Now · September 2026
now.title: Building General Formation
now.body: I am a founding engineer on an AI agent suite for one-person companies. We are exploring how far a coherent agent team can take a business—from a thin idea to grounded strategy, identity, software, and launch material.
now.question: Current question: how much of a small company can an agent team operate without hiding the consequential decisions from its founder?

about: I have spent years studying motivation, behavioral design, and engagement, then applying those ideas to real products. I co-founded CustomerGlu and built its gamification SDK from scratch; it eventually reached more than 150 million devices.

After CustomerGlu, I took one deliberate exploratory chapter: product and growth work at Lingotune, the One Person Growth Team, Distill, and a series of AI-assisted product experiments. The common thread was learning how a small, high-agency team could research, build, grow, and learn faster.
Today I prefer hands-on building to managing large teams. I work across product judgment, research, design, engineering, and the operating systems that let those disciplines compound.

work.title: General Formation
work.summary: An AI agent suite for one-person companies.
work.lead: General Formation takes a founder's intent and coordinates specialist agents to turn it into inspectable business work—not just an answer in a chat window.

cover.alt: Generated Akar concept statement: Akar is a mobile smoothie cart in Bali that puts island-native superfoods.
cover.caption: A statement card produced during a completed General Formation run. Akar is a generated business concept, not an operating company.

sections.title: The question
sections.body: Can a small company gain real operating leverage from agents without giving up founder judgment, taste, or visibility into what happened?

sections.title: What I am building
sections.body: I work across the product experience and the underlying constellation: planning, specialist handoffs, evaluation gates, resumable runs, and a terminal cockpit where a founder can steer the work.

sections.title: A working receipt
sections.body: One completed run turned the thin prompt “Build a business which creates green, healthy smoothies in Bali” into Akar: a grounded product wedge, brand system, social assets, and a rendered responsive site.

sections.title: Truth boundary
sections.body: Akar is evidence of the system producing a coherent business concept and launch-ready collateral. It is not an operating smoothie company, and I do not present it as one.

work.title: CustomerGlu
work.summary: Gamification infrastructure for consumer apps, co-founded and built from scratch.
work.lead: CustomerGlu made it possible for consumer product teams to run native gamified journeys—streaks, challenges, rewards, and campaigns—without rebuilding the machinery each time.

sections.title: What I owned
sections.body: I co-founded the company and built its gamification SDK and platform from scratch, working across product, engineering, behavioral design, customers, and the company itself.

sections.title: The deeper thread
sections.body: The work was an applied study of motivation: not gamification as decoration, but how feedback, goals, progress, rewards, and timing change what people do inside products.

sections.title: Scale
sections.body: The SDK eventually reached more than 150 million devices through consumer apps in India and Southeast Asia.

work.title: Fable Low Power Mode
work.summary: A quota-aware way to save frontier-model time for judgment rather than shell work.
work.lead: A Claude Code skill that watches live usage windows and shifts repetitive execution to cheaper workers when frontier-model quota gets tight.

sections.title: The problem
sections.body: My best model was spending limited quota on file reads, searches, builds, tests, and repetitive edits—the work around the decisions rather than the decisions themselves.

sections.title: The mechanism
sections.body: Low Power Mode reads the 5-hour and 7-day usage percentages already present in Claude Code's statusline payload. At a threshold, it keeps the frontier model focused on planning, judgment, review, and final decisions while subagents handle execution.

sections.title: Observed result
sections.body: For the same working pattern, my Fable allowance moved from roughly two days to at least five. That is a personal workflow measurement, not a universal benchmark.

work.title: LLM Wiki Compiler
work.summary: Turns a folder of notes into a compact, topic-based wiki for coding agents.
work.lead: A Claude Code plugin that compiles large Markdown knowledge folders into smaller topic articles, following the LLM knowledge-base pattern described by Andrej Karpathy.

sections.title: The problem
sections.body: Agent sessions were repeatedly loading large, overlapping context files. The useful knowledge was there, but the shape was expensive and difficult to navigate.

sections.title: What it does
sections.body: The compiler groups source notes by topic, synthesizes them into linked wiki articles, and gives agents a smaller map from which to pull only the context they need.

sections.title: A concrete run
sections.body: One corpus of 383 notes compiled into 13 topic articles. The repository had 311 GitHub stars when this entry was updated on 12 August 2026.

work.title: Cache Audit
work.summary: Finds the parts of a Claude Code setup that are quietly breaking prompt caching.
work.lead: A focused audit skill that checks a Claude Code setup against prompt-caching rules and returns a scored report with specific fixes.

sections.title: Why
sections.body: Prompt caching failures are expensive but mostly invisible. A setup can look normal while volatile context, ordering, or configuration choices keep invalidating the reusable prefix.

sections.title: What it does
sections.body: Cache Audit inspects the setup, explains which rule each issue violates, and turns the diagnosis into concrete changes rather than generic token-saving advice.

work.title: Stoicism Daily
work.summary: A small daily experiment in making Stoic ideas easier to encounter.
work.lead: A lightweight daily Stoic experience that packages an old idea into a contemporary visual prompt and a repeatable ritual.

sections.title: The experiment
sections.body: I wanted to see whether philosophical practice could feel immediate rather than instructional: one small encounter, delivered regularly, with almost no setup.

sections.title: Current form
sections.body: The live site publishes a daily visual Stoic prompt and lets people subscribe for the next one.

reading.title: Generative Agents: Interactive Simulacra of Human Behavior
reading.summary: A visual walk-through of how memory, retrieval, reflection, and planning make an LLM character coherent over time.
reading.tldr: An LLM can make a character sound believable once. This paper adds a notebook, selective attention, reflection, and planning so the character can carry a day forward.
reading.lead: Park et al. ask what it takes to make a computational character believable beyond a single prompt. Their answer is an architecture that carries experience forward: a memory stream, selective retrieval, reflection, planning, and a world that can push back.
reading.takeaway: Believable behavior comes from managing time and state around the model.
reading.subtitle: Interactive Simulacra of Human Behavior

story.headline: A town wakes up. One idea moves through it.
story.intro: Smallville is not interesting because its people can talk. It is interesting because they carry yesterday into today, then change the day for one another.

scenes.title: A want
scenes.body: Isabella wakes up with one idea: throw a Valentine’s Day party.

scenes.title: A memory
scenes.body: She tells Maria. That conversation becomes a fact Isabella and Maria can carry forward.

scenes.title: A ripple
scenes.body: Maria tells Sam. The invitation is no longer only Isabella’s plan; it is now part of the town’s social fabric.

scenes.title: A conflict
scenes.body: Sam finishes work. He knows about the party, but his evening already has a shape.

scenes.title: An imperfect result
scenes.body: Thirteen people know about the party. Only five of the twelve invitees show up.

use_cases.label: Games
use_cases.body: Characters who remember what you did, not just answer the latest line.

use_cases.label: Social worlds
use_cases.body: A way to watch news, invitations, trust, and plans move through a group.

use_cases.label: What you could build
use_cases.body: A small model of a team or community before changing the real one.

principles.title: The world has facts
principles.body: There is a clock, a place, other people, and rules about what can happen.

principles.title: A person sees only part of it
principles.body: Isabella does not know everything in town. She knows what she noticed or what someone told her.

principles.title: Experience becomes memory
principles.body: Important events are saved so the past can affect a later choice.

principles.title: Memory changes the next action
principles.body: The person uses a few relevant memories to decide what to do now.

principles.title: Actions create new facts
principles.body: A conversation, arrival, or missed appointment changes what everyone else can notice next.

build_steps.title: Make the world before the intelligence
build_steps.body: Create one place, a clock, a few activities, and one event. Make sure time and consequences work without a language model.

build_steps.title: Give one person a notebook
build_steps.body: Save what they saw, what they want, and what happened to them. This is the beginning of continuity.

build_steps.title: Let the person choose
build_steps.body: Show the person the current situation and a few relevant memories. Ask for one possible next action, then check that action against the world’s rules.

build_steps.title: Let consequences spread
build_steps.body: Add four more people. A conversation should create a new fact that another person can notice, remember, and act on.

build_steps.title: Add patterns later
build_steps.body: Only after the basic loop works, add daily plans and broader reflections about relationships, habits, and goals.

sections.title: The question
sections.body: An LLM can answer plausibly in the moment, but without continuity it can forget an election, flatten a person into a stereotype, or eat lunch twice. The paper treats memory and time as an architecture problem, not just a prompting problem.

sections.title: What the experiment shows
sections.body: In Smallville, 25 agents accumulate experiences, form relationships, diffuse information, and coordinate around a Valentine’s Day party. Human evaluators preferred the full architecture over versions with reflection, planning, or memory access removed.

sections.title: What it does not show
sections.body: The result is a believable simulacrum in a small, two-day sandbox—not consciousness, human-level understanding, or robust long-term autonomy. Retrieval failures, hallucinated embellishments, over-polite dialogue, missing world norms, and inference cost remain visible boundaries.

reading.title: A review round is a unit of time
reading.display: a review round is a unit of time
reading.summary: One pull request took eight reviewer rounds and 26.5 hours. Four days later one in the same arc merged in 4.3 hours. What changed was the price of a round, not the findings.

reading.title: Jev replaces the decision, never the eyes or the pen
reading.display: jev replaces the decision, never the eyes or the pen
reading.summary: A classifier that never writes, only picks from a menu code already built. The same loop across a browser agent, a voice command, a day of my own screen text, and the one gate in Garage I would hand it next.

updates.title: Jev replaces the decision, never the eyes or the pen
updates.body: Wrote up the classifier I keep putting in front of actions: it never generates text, it only picks from a menu the code already built. Includes a live Calculator run that took six picks at 98 to 100 percent for $0.00021, and the one Garage gate I would hand it next. Five diagrams.

updates.title: A review round is a unit of time
updates.body: Wrote up two weeks of merged pull requests with one human reviewer. Median merge time fell from 17.5 to 8.7 hours while rounds per PR stayed near three: the round got cheaper, not rarer. Five diagrams.

updates.title: Fable Low Power Mode
updates.body: Published the quota-aware skill I use to keep frontier-model time focused on judgment. For the same workflows, my allowance moved from roughly two days to at least five.

updates.title: Akar, a General Formation run
updates.body: A one-line smoothie-business prompt became a grounded product wedge, identity, social assets, and a responsive site. It is a system output—not a claim that the physical business launched.

updates.title: Cache Audit
updates.body: Made prompt-cache failures inspectable: a scored audit of what is burning Claude tokens and why.
